solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Office of the President, where a load of balls may be witnessed

definitions.note: Neither half is a plain synonym of the answer: the President's room is known by the shape of it and the cricket ground by the shape of the field, so the word stands in each case as a name rather than a description.
definitions.meaning: the room in the West Wing where an American president works, known by its shape

definitions.text: where a load of balls may be witnessed
definitions.meaning: a Test cricket ground by Vauxhall in south London, where deliveries are bowled all summer

explanation.surface: The White House office as a place where an enormous amount of nonsense gets talked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A load of balls' is the dismissive phrase the surface wants and the literal count the second definition needs. The comma after 'President' looks like a pause in one sentence and is actually the seam between two whole clues.
explanation.definitionFit: The President's room and the south London cricket ground are both named for their shape, so one word names each.

clue.text: One very contorted bra's pressure line

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
so means very

indicators.note: contorted means the letters of bra are twisted into a new order

parts.note: the word bra, with the 's read as is

explanation.surface: A seriously twisted brassiere is blamed for a line on a chart.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining points of equal atmospheric pressure.

clue.text: Cry: "Women are sick!"

parts.note: w is the letter on the door of the ladies'
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: An outcry at the news that the women have all gone down with something.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the exclamation mark dress the second half up as reported speech, which is exactly what a cry would be. Nothing in the clue admits that the first word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To wail is to cry aloud in grief, and the noun and the verb both answer to it.

clue.text: Indian cookery clubs of Estonia?

parts.note: a balti is a curry cooked and brought to the table in its own steel bowl, a Birmingham invention
c is the card player's short form for clubs

explanation.surface: Curry houses and nightclubs somewhere in an Estonian city.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is apologising for naming a whole region by one of the three countries in it. 'Clubs' sits beside a restaurant and belongs to a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is one of the three Baltic states, so the adjective for the whole region is defined by a single instance of it.

clue.text: Wealthy American goes after Will's character

indicators.note: What goes after a thing follows it, so the short piece named first in the clue is written last, behind the long one.

parts.note: the exiled duke who works the magic in Shakespeare's The Tempest
US is the everyday short form for American

explanation.surface: A rich American trailing round after one of Shakespeare's creations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' is Shakespeare on first-name terms, a habit worth learning because setters use it constantly. The clue reads left to right while the answer assembles the other way, which is what 'goes after' is there to warn you about.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosperous means thriving and comfortably off, which is what calling somebody wealthy says.

clue.text: Marks and Spencer's chief at AGM — it's chaotic

indicators.note: The chief of a word is the letter at its head, so only the first letter of the name before it is taken.

parts.note: the letter standing at the head of the name

indicators.note: Chaos is the absence of any arrangement at all, so the letters gathered up in front of it hold no order of their own.

parts.note: the little word taken exactly as printed
the three letters of the annual general meeting, taken as printed
the pronoun taken exactly as printed

explanation.surface: A high-street retailer's boss making a shambles of the annual general meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks and Spencer's chief' reads as one man running one shop and splits straight down the middle, the definition on one side and a single letter on the other. Stigmata are the wounds of the Crucifixion, reappearing on the hands and feet of saints.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigmata are marks on the body, so the plural noun answers the plural noun.

clue.text: Balls after tense jog

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the word opening the clue takes second place.

parts.note: t is the grammarian's short form for tense
rot is talk not worth listening to

explanation.surface: Nonsense talked after somebody's nervous little run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' and 'rot' are both words for nonsense, which is the sense the wordplay wants and not the one the capital letter at the front of the clue invites. Tense is a property of verbs before it is a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A trot is a gentle run, which is what a jog is; both work as noun and as verb.

clue.text: Eye-related American reversal in medication aid?

indicators.note: in puts the reversed letters inside the small bottle

parts.note: a vial is a small bottle that holds medicine

indicators.note: reversal means turning round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

explanation.surface: A policy U-turn by the Americans on a drug that helps eyesight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversal' turns US into SU, which goes 'in' VIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Visual describes anything to do with sight, the function of the eye.

clue.text: Teller's list Republican managed to overturn

indicators.note: To overturn a thing is to tip it upside down, and in an across entry that means the whole assembly is read back from its right-hand end.

parts.note: a rota is the list saying whose turn it is
r is the standard short form for Republican, as on an American ballot
to run a department is to manage it

explanation.surface: A bank cashier's duty roster that a Republican contrived to get thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teller' is the bank counter on the surface and the storyteller in the definition. All three pieces go in facing forwards and the finished run is turned round once at the end, rather than each piece separately.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrator is the one who tells the story, so teller names the job exactly.

clue.text: Our ex-PM "right off the French" — scrap

indicators.note: Taking something off is taking it away, so the letter just named comes out of the word in front of it.

parts.note: Liz Truss, Britain's Prime Minister for seven weeks in the autumn of 2022
r is the standard short form for right, as in a stage direction
le is one of the French words for the

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister dropping her rightwing politics along with the French.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'right off the French' look like one soundbite and hide the join: the first word is a letter to lose, the last two a word to gain. French articles are standard crossword currency — LE, LA, UN, UNE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tussle is a rough physical struggle, and a scrap is that same scuffle under a more casual name.

clue.text: Private Eye would rather not have one be ill dancing at clubs

definitions.text: Private Eye would rather not have one

indicators.note: dancers move about, so the letters move into a new order

parts.note: clubs is one suit in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A satirical magazine joke: feeling sick while dancing at nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges BE ILL, and SUIT (clubs being a card suit) follows; 'at' is a link. Private Eye, the British satirical magazine, is famous for being sued for defamation.
explanation.definitionFit: A defamation claim in court is the legal action a satirical magazine most dreads facing.

clue.text: This is about grabbing money — which makes sense

indicators.note: grabbing means holding hold of, so the rearranged word closes round the money letter
is about means is around and in disorder, so the letters are turned round into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the letters of this
G stands for grand, a thousand pounds, so money

explanation.surface: A cynic remarks that some scheme is a money grab, which adds up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges THIS into SIHT, which is 'grabbing' G for money. 'Which makes sense' reads as agreement; only 'sense' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight is one of the five senses, alongside hearing, touch, taste and smell.

clue.text: (&15/17) Yet forecast starts off with "fire Burnham's close colleague!"

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off has turned, and letters told they are off have turned too: not one of them stays where it was printed.

parts.note: seventeen letters from these three words, every one of them used
four more letters thrown onto the same pile

explanation.surface: A weather forecast that opens by demanding the sacking of the mayor's closest ally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts off with' reads as one phrase meaning 'begins with', and only the middle word of it is an instruction. Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July 2026, which is what makes his closest colleague a cabinet rank rather than a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: The First Secretary of State outranks the rest of the cabinet as the Prime Minister's de facto deputy, and Andy Burnham is that Prime Minister.

clue.text: Base weakness of speaker

indicators.note: What belongs to a speaker is a sound rather than a spelling, so the word wanted is one you hear and then write down differently.

parts.note: a flaw is a weakness, and British speech sounds no r at the end of a word

explanation.surface: A fault in the way somebody speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Speaker of the Commons is the decoy, and the floor is where members speak. The two words only sound alike in British English, where that final r is left unsounded.
explanation.definitionFit: The floor is the base of a room, the surface everything else in it stands on.

clue.text: They could well be toxic, contemptible types and dicks

definitions.note: The definition is a clause about the answer rather than a synonym for it: it states the one thing the name is meant to warn you of, since the word marks no botanical category of its own.

parts.note: a toad is a person you would rather not share a room with
tool is the same playground insult as dick, and both started from the same anatomical joke

explanation.surface: A roll-call of unpleasant people, with a warning that they may be poisonous as well.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are playground insults, which is this setter's register throughout the puzzle. 'Types' looks like a category word and is doing nothing of the kind — it is only what makes the toads plural.
explanation.definitionFit: English calls a mushroom a toadstool precisely when it is thought poisonous, so the name carries the warning rather than any botanical distinction.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Tory ultimately lied about produce

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of Tory is picked out

indicators.note: about means around and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician finally told falsehoods about farm output.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes Y from TORY, and 'about' rearranges LIED into IELD.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm's yield is its produce, the crop or output it gives.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Dodgy cures and IT associated with Kennedy's "ultimate protection"

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable, so these letters are rearranged
ultimate means last, so only the final letter of the name is used

parts.note: the name Kennedy, whose ultimate letter is taken

explanation.surface: Quack remedies and computing were linked to the late President Kennedy's final safeguard.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'ultimate protection' look like a Kennedy phrase, but 'ultimate' only picks the last letter of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Security is a state of safety from threat, so it is a synonym of protection.

clue.text: Material of robe forced round arse

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go on either side of the scoundrel
forced means pushed out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: in British slang an arse is a contemptible fool, much like a cad, a man who behaves dishonourably

explanation.surface: A garment's fabric is pulled tight around someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forced' rearranges ROBE into BROE, which goes 'round' CAD. 'Arse' is British slang for an idiot, much like a cad.
explanation.definitionFit: Brocade is a rich woven fabric with a raised pattern, often of silk or gold thread.

clue.text: Charitable African country protecting government leader

indicators.note: To protect a thing is to stand round it, so the country's letters close over the one named after them.

parts.note: Benin is the narrow West African state between Togo and Nigeria

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so only the first letter of the word in front is taken.

parts.note: the letter standing at the head of that word

explanation.surface: A generous West African state looking after its head of government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Protecting government leader' reads as one job description and is two separate instructions laid end to end. The single letter goes in one place from the end, which is the only slot that leaves a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Benign means kindly and well disposed, the temperament a charitable person shows.

clue.text: When MPs break Mone's heart about PPI's ultimate decline

parts.note: Parliament's holiday periods are called recesses

indicators.note: about suggests turning round, so the end letter is brought round to the front
the heart of Mone is its two middle letters
ultimate means last, so the final letter of PPI

explanation.surface: A Private Eye jab at Baroness Mone and the PPE contracts row while Parliament is off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rotates ONI, the heart of Mone plus the end of PPI, bringing the I round to the front. Michelle Mone is a peer caught up in a scandal over pandemic protective equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: An economic recession is a downturn, a period of decline in output.

clue.text: Prompt Victor to usurp Charlie's request

indicators.note: to usurp is to seize another's place, so one letter takes over the position of the other

parts.note: to incite someone is to prompt or urge them to act
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone urges a man named Victor to seize power at Charlie's request.
explanation.walkthrough: V 'to usurp' C in INCITE.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun in informal English, an invite is a request to attend, short for invitation.

clue.text: Quiet, extreme leftwinger's piece

parts.note: sh is the noise made to hush somebody
red has meant a communist since the Russian revolution

explanation.surface: A hushed remark about a hard-left politician's contribution.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after the first word does real work, keeping it from being swallowed into the description of the politician. This is the smallest kind of piece there is, which is why the word turns up in 'not a shred of evidence'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shred is a torn-off scrap, so it is a piece of something — usually the very smallest piece going.

clue.text: Old president Trump needs to change party

indicators.note: switching party from Democrat to Republican means the letter for one party is swapped for the other's

parts.note: Donald Trump, the US president
D stands for Democrat
R stands for Republican

explanation.surface: A satirical swipe suggesting Trump ought to defect to the other political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change party' swaps D (Democrat) in DONALD for R (Republican), giving a different Republican president.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan was US president in the 1980s, so he is an earlier holder of the office.

clue.text: Old Hollywood star's flipping tabloid stink

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the word after it is read from its last letter back to its first.

parts.note: BO is body odour, the two letters a century of British advertising made unmentionable
a rag is a newspaper nobody respects, and it arrives here back to front

explanation.surface: A screen legend furious about a smelly newspaper story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is a mild British swearword as well as an instruction, which is why it sits so comfortably in front of 'tabloid'. Greta Garbo walked away from Hollywood at thirty-six and never went back.
explanation.definitionFit: Greta Garbo was the Swedish star of the silent era and the early talkies, so the surname alone names an old Hollywood star.

clue.text: MAGA means suppressing contest

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down out of sight, so what is wanted is already sitting inside the words as printed.

parts.note: four letters running in order across the space between these two words, starting two letters into the first

explanation.surface: A political slogan quietly shutting down any argument.
explanation.walkthrough: MAGA is the Trump campaign slogan and 'means' looks like the start of a definition of it. Nothing needs converting here — the letters are already written out, just not where the eye stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A game is a contest played to rules, so the two words name one thing from the playful side and the competitive side.

clue.text: A living ruined by the heartless anti-migrant activist?

indicators.note: ruined means the letters of a living are wrecked and rebuilt
heartless means the's middle letter is removed, leaving its outside

explanation.surface: A livelihood wrecked by a callous anti-immigration campaigner.
explanation.definitionFit: A vigilante takes the law into their own hands, as some self-appointed border patrollers do.

clue.text: US enforcers going after "Liberal lousy things"

indicators.note: What goes after a thing comes behind it, so the three letters named first are written second, following the single one.

parts.note: l is the standard short form for Liberal, as on a ballot paper
ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the American agency that carries out deportation raids

explanation.surface: Immigration agents coming down hard on a liberal for calling things lousy.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks turn the last three words into a jeer somebody is being punished for, and in the parse they split unevenly: one word is a letter and two are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lice are the parasites that the adjective lousy was made from, so the phrase names them through the word they gave English.

clue.text: All but advanced peer

indicators.note: 'All but' means nearly all of a thing, so the word after it is taken short of its final letter.

parts.note: an advanced warning is an early one, and this word loses its tail

explanation.surface: A member of the Lords who was very nearly given a step up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All but advanced' reads as one description of a man who missed out, and the first two words are an instruction aimed at the third. An earl sits in the middle of the five ranks of the peerage.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is one of the ranks of the British peerage, so 'peer' defines by the class he belongs to.

clue.text: Butcher's dog cut one on behind

indicators.note: cut means the word is docked, losing its last letter

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog
the final T of the dog's name
I is the Roman numeral for one
behind, as in behind schedule, means late

explanation.surface: Reads as an account of a butcher's dog tail-docked and running late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' docks the dog's last letter, as a tail is docked; 'Butcher' is a verb here, not the tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: To butcher something is to hack it about savagely, which is what mutilating does.

clue.text: Eye's description of comical leader given the boot

definitions.note: an adjective describing things relating to the eye

indicators.note: the leader, the opening letter, is kicked out

parts.note: jocular means joking, comical

explanation.surface: Private Eye describes itself as a comic magazine whose leader has been sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: Eye refers to the eye, not the magazine Private Eye. JOCULAR loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocular means relating to the eye, so it is the adjective used to describe an eye.
